before.content:
A small business can begin a security review by identifying what the website stores, who can change it and how service is restored after a failure. A padlock or a familiar platform name does not answer those questions.

Inventory the information and operations that need protection

Internet-facing websites can receive automated probes for known weaknesses as well as targeted attacks. This article does not establish the proportion affecting Mumbai small businesses. Inventory exposed services, supported software and administrative access before choosing protections. A lack of visible symptoms is not proof that no attempt or compromise occurred.

Use transport security without mistaking it for authorisation

HTTPS uses TLS to protect data in transit when correctly configured. A valid certificate is one part of that connection, not a complete application-security assessment. Review server access controls, software dependencies, credentials and recovery too. A secure connection alone does not make a form or stored record safe.

Can I handle website security myself, or do I need to hire someone?

The basics — SSL, strong passwords, 2FA — are usually things you can set up yourself with a bit of guidance. Ongoing monitoring, update management, and responding to an actual breach are usually better handled by someone experienced, since mistakes there can make things worse.

Test the recovery path as well as the backup job

If your site gets hacked, a plugin update breaks something, or someone on your team accidentally deletes a page, a recent backup is the difference between a five-minute fix and rebuilding from scratch. The basics that matter:

  • Backups should run automatically, not depend on someone remembering to do it manually.
  • They should be stored somewhere separate from your live site — a backup sitting on the same hacked server doesn't help you.
  • Test them occasionally. A backup nobody's ever restored from is a backup you're only assuming works.

Review dependency changes and unsupported components

Known software vulnerabilities are one important exposure to investigate, alongside credentials, configuration, access controls and integrations. This guide does not establish which cause accounts for most small-business incidents. Inventory supported versions and apply relevant security updates through a tested release process. Managed services, custom builds and plugin-based sites all require attention to their actual dependencies. A patched component does not prove that the entire application is safe.

Assign account access to real responsibilities

"admin123" is still shockingly common on small business site logins, and it's one of the easiest doors for an automated attack to walk through. A few basics go a long way:

  • Use a genuinely strong, unique password for your website admin — not the same one you use for five other accounts.
  • Use an appropriate second factor where supported, protect recovery methods and restrict privileged access. Multi-factor authentication can reduce some credential risks but does not prevent every attack or repair record-level authorisation. Review sessions, recovery and phishing-resistant options for the actual account system instead of treating a second prompt as a complete defence.
  • Limit login attempts so a bot can't just guess passwords repeatedly.

Choose observable signals and an escalation route

Unexpected redirects, unfamiliar accounts and unexplained content changes warrant investigation. An illustrative plugin compromise can explain the risk, but this guide does not document a named SiteNova client's incident. Preserve evidence, restrict affected access and use qualified incident support rather than diagnose the cause from a traffic drop alone.

Budget ownership rather than an implied guarantee

Budget the actual security responsibilities, including updates, access review, restoration tests and incident response. Neither prevention nor cleanup has a universal cost for every small business. Prioritise the consequences of the specific exposure and identify support before an incident. A meaningful review reports its coverage and remaining limits instead of declaring the whole website protected.

Test with two ordinary accounts

For any private feature, verify that one account cannot read another customer's record by changing an identifier. Hiding an admin link does not enforce that boundary. Review logs and error monitoring for accidental secrets or personal data. Keep public uploads separate from private documents and validate access on the server. These checks do not prove complete security, but they can reveal specific failures that a visual review of the login page will miss.

How do I know if my website already has SSL set up?

Check that the intended hostname uses a valid HTTPS connection and inspect any browser warning. HTTPS protects the connection; it does not prove that the business is legitimate, the application is free of vulnerabilities or private data is correctly authorised. Modern browser icons vary, so do not treat a padlock graphic as a complete security test.

How often should backups actually run?

Set backup frequency and retention against the amount of work the business can afford to lose and how long recovery may take. Verify what the provider includes, keep an appropriate separate recovery copy and test restoration. A static brochure and an active order ledger should not inherit the same schedule without reviewing their data-loss consequences.

My website is small — am I really a target?

Yes. Most attacks aren't personal or targeted; they're automated scans looking for any site with an unpatched vulnerability. Size doesn't make you invisible to that kind of scan.

What's the very first thing I should check today?

Check the HTTPS connection and supported software versions as starting tasks, then inspect access controls, credentials, exposed services and backups. Those initial checks do not establish that most vulnerabilities were found. Record what was tested and what remains outside the review, with an owner for addressing confirmed issues.

Use a concrete access test as part of review: one customer must not retrieve another customer's record by changing its identifier. Test through the real application path and inspect response caching. A login screen and an encrypted connection do not establish that record-level authorisation works. Keep the result and any untested boundary in the handover record rather than label the entire site secure after a single browser check.
